Play basketball in America

Two kids from our gym on Østerbro have gone to North America. We coached them both for years before they went. Now we are adding help with the move itself: we get the player ready, then we help get them there.

Email Coach Deng

Every player named

Some placement websites show a 99 percent success rate and cannot name one kid they sent anywhere. Every player we help goes on this page by name, with the school and the year.

Malthe joined our Academy for the year and we ran the process with him. He went to Fort Erie International Academy and then Orangeville Prep in Ontario. Valdemar played for Talata Men, and we set up his move to The Patrick School basketball program in New Jersey this fall. Johan came up through the club from the very first season. We built the player, and his family ran the move.

Who does what. We do the evaluation, the film, the profile and the relationship, because we see the player every week. The placement itself runs through licensed partner agencies, who handle school matching, admissions and the visa. We stay in it the whole way, and we stay on the phone once they land.

Two more players have gone from our men's side into the Danish 1. division. That is a step up at home, so they are on the pathway page.

Routes

Most families arrive asking about one of these, and often it is the wrong one for now. First we work out which road the player is on.

High school and prep, USA and Canada

The most common way into American college basketball, and the road Johan is on. School matching, admissions, host family or dorm, and the visa paperwork that comes with it.

USA · Canada

Clubs and academies in Europe

Sometimes the right step up is a short flight away. Spanish and other European academies take young players seriously, the basketball education is excellent, and a fifteen year old stays in the same time zone as home.

Spain · Europe

College basketball in the USA

NCAA Division 1 and 2, NAIA and JUCO. Eligibility, academics and tape, sorted early. The academic side ends more of these than the basketball side does.

USA

These are programmes and coaches we can reach, not sponsors and not endorsements. Our Canada camp runs in Lethbridge, Coach Deng played at Mount Royal in Calgary and Coach Jordan played Division 1 at Wyoming, which is where a lot of the Alberta side of this comes from.

How it works

It starts with a conversation between you, the player and Deng. What the family wants and what the player wants can be two different things, and it is better to find that out now.

Then an evaluation from the coaches who see the player every week, with measured numbers. If the answer is "not yet", you hear it here. The conversation and the evaluation are free.

Before anyone commits, you get a plan with the full cost on it: tuition, flights, insurance, all of it, up front.

Then the profile and film: a measured profile sheet, a cut highlight reel, and full games, uncut. The reel gets a coach to look. The full games show what a player does when the ball is somewhere else.

We go to programmes we know, or ones our contacts in that market know. Fit comes first. The biggest name is the wrong name for most players.

Admissions, visa and landing are handled by our partner agency, with us in every conversation. We stay in touch once they are out there, because the first three months abroad are the hard bit.

Who does this

Deng Awak

Head coach. Founded Talata in 2021, coached both of the players above, and sits in every one of these conversations himself.

Jordan Naughton

Played NCAA Division 1 at the University of Wyoming, then turned pro in Denmark with BK Amager. He coaches our Academy. When a fifteen year old asks what it takes, Jordan answers.

Partner agencies

The placement process runs through established agencies we work with, including FIBA licensed representation. The club is the coach, the agency is the agent.

Coming in 2027: NIL. American college athletes can earn from their name, image and likeness now, and the rules for international athletes are moving fast. We are building that into the advice.

Ground rules

  • We tell you when your kid is not ready. A clear answer is the most useful thing on this page.
  • Nobody can promise a scholarship. We won't, and anyone who does is selling you something.
  • You get names you can check. We never put a percentage on it.
  • It has to be right for the player, at the right age. Being able to afford it is no reason to send a young player abroad. Done wrong, it is an expensive way to fall out of love with the game.

Questions

  • How does a Danish player end up in an American high school? Almost always through prep or high school first, then college. You need tape, measured numbers, school grades and someone on the other end who knows the programme. That is the whole job.
  • How old should they be? Fifteen or sixteen is the usual window for high school and prep. Younger than that and we will normally tell you to wait, and why.
  • What does it cost? It depends on the school and how much aid comes with it. You get the full number, including flights and insurance, before anyone signs anything.
  • Will they get a scholarship? Maybe. We won't promise it and neither should anybody else.
  • What if they're not good enough yet? Then we say so and tell you what to work on. Most players who ask us are not ready in the first year. That is a "not yet", not a no forever.
  • Can they come home? Yes, and some do. Malthe went to Canada for a year and came back. That year still counts.
  • Do they need to be a Talata player? Players from any club in Denmark can ask us for a read. Get in touch.
